- A watch is set after a change happened. The one-shot watch never fires, so a client misses an update. Mitigate by reading the value and setting the watch in the same call.
terms.codeSnippet:
# zkCli.sh: ephemeral znode for broker registration
create /brokers
create -e /brokers/broker-1 "10.0.1.5:9092"
ls -w /brokers

# leader election with sequential ephemeral nodes
create -e -s /election/candidate- "broker-1"
ls /election
# lowest sequence number, e.g. candidate-0000000003, is the leader

# zoo.cfg for a 3-node ensemble
tickTime=2000
server.1=zk1:2888:3888
server.2=zk2:2888:3888
server.3=zk3:2888:3888

terms.definition: A data processing architecture that maintains two parallel pipelines: a batch layer that periodically reprocesses all historical data for accuracy, and a speed (streaming) layer that processes new events in near-real time for low latency. A serving layer merges results from both. The main disadvantage is maintaining two separate codebases that must produce equivalent output.
terms.example: An ad-click aggregation system uses a nightly MapReduce batch job over all raw click data for accurate billing, alongside a Flink streaming job for near-real-time click counts. If the streaming layer has a bug, the batch layer's output overrides it at end of day — but any fix must be applied and tested in both codebases independently.
terms.howItWorks:
Every event is written twice, once to an immutable master dataset in storage like HDFS or S3 and once to a stream such as Kafka.

The batch layer runs on a schedule, often nightly. It recomputes views from the full master dataset with Spark or MapReduce. The speed layer, in Flink or Storm, updates a small real-time view from events that arrived since the last batch run.

The serving layer answers queries by merging the two. For a query on today's counts it reads the batch view up to the last run timestamp and adds the speed view after it. When a new batch finishes, the speed layer's data for that range is discarded, so any streaming bug is overwritten.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Batch recomputation corrects any past error, but you write and test the same logic twice, in two frameworks.
- Fresh numbers come within seconds from the speed layer, while exact numbers arrive only after the next batch, up to a day later.
- Running both layers doubles cluster cost and on-call surface.
- Kappa architecture removes the second codebase, and needs a log with long retention and fast replay.
terms.failureModes:
- The batch and speed code drift. Dashboards show a number that jumps when the batch lands. Share business logic in a library and compare outputs in CI.
- The batch job overruns its window. The merge boundary moves and the serving layer double counts or drops the overlap. Track the boundary timestamp explicitly and alarm on batch duration.
- A late-arriving event is counted by the speed layer and not by the batch input snapshot. Totals disagree. Define the batch cutoff by event time and re-read late data.
terms.codeSnippet:
-- serving layer: batch view up to the cutoff, speed view after
SELECT ad_id, SUM(clicks) AS clicks FROM (
  SELECT ad_id, clicks FROM batch_view
   WHERE window_end <= (SELECT max(window_end) FROM batch_view)
  UNION ALL
  SELECT ad_id, clicks FROM speed_view
   WHERE window_end > (SELECT max(window_end) FROM batch_view)
) t
GROUP BY ad_id;

terms.definition: A data processing architecture that unifies batch and stream processing into a single streaming pipeline, eliminating the dual-codebase problem of Lambda architecture. Historical data reprocessing is achieved by replaying stored events through the same streaming engine used for real-time data, typically directed to a dedicated aggregation service to avoid impacting live processing.
terms.example: An ad-click aggregation system routes both live Kafka events and historical replays through a single aggregation service. When a bug in aggregation logic is found, the fix is deployed once; the recalculation service replays raw data from cold storage through the corrected pipeline and writes updated results to the aggregation database.
terms.howItWorks:
Kappa keeps one processing path. All events go to a log with long retention, such as Kafka with `retention.ms=-1` or tiered storage. A stream job reads the log and writes a result table.

To change the logic, you deploy the new job version as a second consumer group. It starts at the earliest offset and replays the whole log into a new table. When it has caught up to the tip and its output checks out, you point readers at the new table and stop the old job.

Because both versions run the same engine on the same input, no separate batch code exists. Replays run at the cluster's read speed, often many times real time, and with bounded parallelism so they do not starve the live job.
terms.tradeoffs:
- One codebase replaces two, but the log must retain every event you may ever replay. That costs storage, or tiered storage to object stores.
- Replaying a year of data can take hours, and in that time you run two copies of the job and double the state.
- Stream engines handle exact, large windowed joins less cheaply than a batch engine, so some analytics fit badly.
- Schema changes in old events must stay readable by new code.
terms.failureModes:
- The replay job shares resources with the live job. Live latency climbs during backfill. Run the replay in a separate cluster or with quotas.
- Retention expires part of the history before the fix ships. The rebuilt table is incomplete. Archive raw events to object storage and replay from there.
- The cutover happens before the new table reaches the tip. Readers see stale numbers. Gate the switch on consumer lag near zero.
terms.codeSnippet:
# redeploy v2 as a fresh group that replays from the start
flink run -d aggregator-v2.jar \
  --group.id clicks-agg-v2 \
  --scan.startup.mode earliest-offset \
  --sink.table clicks_agg_v2
# wait until lag is near zero, then flip readers
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server b1:9092 \
  --describe --group clicks-agg-v2
# ALTER VIEW clicks_agg AS SELECT * FROM clicks_agg_v2;

terms.definition: An extension of a time window in stream processing that allows late-arriving events to be included in an aggregation. A watermark extends the logical closing time of a window by a configured delay; events that arrive within the watermark period are still counted, while events that arrive after the window fully closes are either discarded or handled separately by a reconciliation job.
terms.example: An ad-click aggregation uses 1-minute tumbling windows. With a 15-second watermark, a click event timestamped at 12:00:45 that arrives at 12:01:10 (10 seconds late) is still included in the 12:00 window. A longer watermark captures more late events at the cost of higher result latency; leftover discrepancies are caught by an end-of-day reconciliation batch job.
terms.howItWorks:
A watermark is the stream engine's claim that no events older than time T will arrive. The engine tracks the largest event time seen and sets the watermark to that value minus an allowed delay. In Flink, `WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(15))` does exactly this.

A window `[12:00:00, 12:01:00)` stays open and keeps accepting events until the watermark passes 12:01:00. With a 15-second delay that happens when an event stamped 12:01:15 shows up. Then the engine fires the window and emits the result.

Events stamped before the current watermark are late. The engine drops them, routes them to a side output, or applies `allowedLateness` and re-emits an updated result.
terms.tradeoffs:
- A longer delay captures more late events, and every result waits that long to appear. A 15-second delay adds 15 seconds of latency.
- A short delay gives fast results and drops more late data, which you then reconcile in a batch job.
- Side output for late events keeps them without changing emitted windows. You build the correction path.
- With many partitions, the watermark is the minimum across them, so one idle partition holds back every window.
terms.failureModes:
- An idle source partition emits no events. The minimum watermark stalls and windows never fire. Symptom is no output at night. Set an idle timeout such as `withIdleness(Duration.ofMinutes(1))`.
- Mobile clients upload after hours offline. Their events fall far behind the watermark and vanish from counts. Send them to a late side output and reconcile.
- A producer with a skewed clock writes timestamps in the future. The watermark jumps ahead and every normal event is marked late. Validate or clamp timestamps on ingest.

terms.definition: A small fixed-size image (typically 256×256 pixels) representing a bounded geographic area at a specific zoom level. The world is pre-divided into a grid of tiles; at each zoom level the tile count quadruples. Clients download only the tiles visible in the current viewport, and tiles are pre-computed, stored in object storage, and served from CDN edge nodes to minimize latency.
terms.example: At zoom level 0 the entire world is a single 256×256 tile. Google Maps pre-computes tiles across all zoom levels — estimated at roughly 70 petabytes compressed. A user navigating in Tokyo fetches tiles from the nearest CDN point-of-presence, reducing round-trip time from ~180 ms (origin in us-east-1) to ~8 ms.
terms.howItWorks:
In the common Web Mercator scheme the world at zoom `z` is a grid of `2^z` by `2^z` tiles, so zoom 0 has 1 tile and zoom 18 has about 69 billion. A tile is addressed by `z/x/y`. To find a tile for a latitude and longitude, the client converts to Mercator, scales by `2^z`, and floors the results into `x` and `y`.

The viewport is a rectangle of pixels. The client works out which `x,y` pairs it covers (a few dozen at 256 pixels each on a typical screen) and requests `/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` for each, in parallel. Servers pre-render raster tiles or serve vector tiles in Mapbox Vector Tile format, which are protobuf blobs the client draws itself. Popular tiles are cached in the CDN, and rarely viewed zoom levels may be rendered on first request and stored.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Pre-rendering makes serving a plain static file lookup. Storage grows by about 4 times per extra zoom level, so deep zooms are often rendered on demand.
- Vector tiles are smaller than PNGs, support rotation and restyling on the client, and scale to high-DPI screens. They need client GPU or CPU to render.
- Fixed `z/x/y` URLs cache perfectly at the CDN. Any data edit means invalidating tiles, often through a short TTL or versioned path.
- A 256 pixel tile gives fine-grained fetching. Larger 512 pixel tiles cut request count by 4 at the price of more wasted pixels at the edge.
terms.failureModes:
- A map style update is deployed under the same tile URLs. CDN and browsers serve a mix of old and new tiles. Version the path, for example `/v42/{z}/{x}/{y}`.
- Panning fast issues hundreds of requests and the tile server saturates. Symptom is gray holes. Cancel requests for tiles out of view and prefetch only a one-tile margin.
- Wrong y-axis convention between TMS (origin at bottom) and XYZ (origin at top) flips the map upside down. Check the scheme of the tileset before serving.

terms.definition: Reducing the resolution of time-series data by aggregating multiple data points into a single value (e.g., averaging 10-second readings into 1-minute buckets). Applied to older data to reduce storage costs while preserving trend information; the rollup schedule is typically configurable and managed by the time-series database or an ETL pipeline.
terms.example: A metrics monitoring system retains raw 10-second CPU readings for 7 days, rolls them up to 1-minute averages for 30 days, and further rolls up to 1-hour averages for 1 year. Six rows per minute become one row — a 6× storage reduction — while engineers can still identify hour-long load trends in historical data.
terms.howItWorks:
A rollup job reads raw points for a time window, groups them into fixed buckets, and writes one aggregate per bucket into a coarser retention tier. For 10-second CPU data and a 1-minute bucket, six samples collapse into one row.

Storing only the average loses peaks. Good rollups keep several aggregates per bucket, such as `min`, `max`, `sum`, and `count`. Averages of averages are only correct when you keep `sum` and `count` and divide at query time. Tiers cascade, so the 1-hour tier is built from the 1-minute tier. The raw tier is then deleted by a retention policy once the rollup is done.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Cuts storage by the bucket ratio, 6 times from 10 seconds to 1 minute and 60 times from 1 minute to 1 hour, but cannot be undone once raw data expires.
- Dashboards over long ranges read far fewer points and load faster.
- Keeping max and min per bucket preserves spikes at 3 to 5 times the storage of average alone.
- Percentiles cannot be rolled up from percentiles. Keep histograms or sketches such as t-digest.
terms.failureModes:
- Averaging averages across unequal sample counts gives wrong values. A graph shows 40% CPU when the true figure is 55%. Store `sum` and `count`.
- The rollup job falls behind or fails and raw data expires first. Permanent gaps appear in the long-term tier. Alert on rollup lag and set retention longer than the job delay.
- Alerting rules pointed at the 1-hour tier miss 2-minute spikes. Alert on raw or max series.
terms.codeSnippet:
-- InfluxDB 1.x continuous query: 10s raw -> 1m rollup
CREATE CONTINUOUS QUERY cq_cpu_1m ON metrics BEGIN
  SELECT mean(usage) AS mean, max(usage) AS max, count(usage) AS n
  INTO metrics.rp_30d.cpu_1m
  FROM metrics.rp_7d.cpu
  GROUP BY time(1m), host
END
CREATE RETENTION POLICY rp_7d ON metrics DURATION 7d REPLICATION 1 DEFAULT

terms.definition: A fixed-size, non-overlapping time window in stream processing where each event belongs to exactly one window. When a window closes, all events within it are aggregated and emitted as a result, then the next window starts fresh with no overlap. Used for periodic batch-style aggregations over streaming data where each interval is independent.
terms.example: An ad-click system uses a 1-minute tumbling window: all click events from 12:00:00 to 12:00:59 are collected, the count per ad_id is computed, and results are emitted at 12:01:00. The next window begins at 12:01:00 with a fresh count — no events from the previous window carry over.
terms.howItWorks:
The engine assigns each event to one window by integer division on its timestamp. For a window of size `S`, the start is `ts - (ts % S)`. A click at 12:00:45 with a 60 second window maps to the window starting 12:00:00.

For each key, such as `ad_id`, the engine keeps one accumulator per open window, for example a running count. Each event updates the accumulator for its window and key. State is small, one number per key and window.

When the watermark passes the window end, the engine emits the final value and frees the state. The next window starts at the old end with an empty accumulator. Windows are aligned to the epoch, so all keys share the same boundaries.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Each event is counted once, so aggregation is cheap, but a burst straddling a boundary is split across two windows and looks smaller in each.
- A sliding window fixes that by overlapping, and does `size / slide` times as much work per event.
- Short windows (1 second) give fresh data and many small writes to the sink. Long windows (1 hour) hold more state and delay results.
- Event-time windows are correct under delay. Processing-time windows are simpler and shift results when the pipeline lags.
terms.failureModes:
- Windows use processing time during a backlog. Replayed data lands in the current window and a spike appears at the replay moment. Use event time.
- Time zones or daily windows cut at local midnight in the wrong zone. Daily totals mismatch finance reports. Pick UTC or an explicit zone and document it.
- A very high-cardinality key creates millions of accumulators per window and exhausts state memory. Cap keys or use a state backend such as RocksDB.
terms.codeSnippet:
-- Flink SQL: clicks per ad per 1 minute tumbling window
SELECT
  ad_id,
  window_start,
  window_end,
  COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM TABLE(
  TUMBLE(TABLE clicks, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE))
GROUP BY ad_id, window_start, window_end;

terms.definition: A durability technique that splits data into k data fragments and m parity fragments using a coding scheme (e.g., Reed-Solomon), distributing all k+m fragments across separate nodes so the original data can be reconstructed from any k of them. This tolerates m simultaneous node failures while requiring less storage overhead than full replication.
terms.example: In the S3-like Object Storage design, an 8+4 erasure-coding scheme stores 8 data shards and 4 parity shards across three failure domains, achieving 11 nines of durability with only 50% storage overhead—far below the 200% overhead of 3-way replication.
terms.howItWorks:
The encoder splits an object into `k` equal data shards. It then computes `m` parity shards using Reed-Solomon arithmetic over a Galois field, where each parity shard is a different linear combination of the data shards. All `k+m` shards go to different nodes or racks.

To read, the system fetches any `k` shards. If all data shards arrive, it concatenates them. If some are missing, it solves the linear system using surviving shards to recover the missing ones. With 8+4, you lose up to 4 shards and still read the object. Storage overhead is `m/k`, here 50%. A repair job rebuilds lost shards onto new nodes.
terms.tradeoffs:
- 8+4 stores 1.5 bytes per byte of data against 3 for triple replication, halving disk cost.
- A degraded read must fetch `k` shards and do decode math, so latency and CPU are higher than reading one replica.
- Repair of one lost shard reads `k` shards of data, an 8 times network cost compared with copying one replica. Locally repairable codes reduce this.
- Small objects waste space and IOPS when split. Many stores replicate small objects and erasure-code large ones.
terms.failureModes:
- Correlated failures take out more than `m` shards of one object, such as a rack power loss when shards share the rack. Data becomes unreadable. Place shards across independent failure domains.
- Slow repair after a disk loss leaves objects at reduced redundancy. A second failure then risks data loss. Prioritize repair of the least-redundant objects and monitor repair queue age.
- Silent bit rot goes undetected until read. Store a checksum per shard and scrub on a schedule.
terms.codeSnippet:
# MinIO: set 8 data + 4 parity per erasure set
export MINIO_STORAGE_CLASS_STANDARD="EC:4"
minio server /mnt/disk{1...12}

# Python reedsolo: 4 parity bytes recover 4 erased bytes
from reedsolo import RSCodec
rs = RSCodec(4)
enc = rs.encode(b'hello world')
dec, _, _ = rs.decode(enc[2:])   # two bytes lost, still recovers

terms.definition: A pattern that continuously reads row-level change events (inserts, updates, deletes) from a database's write-ahead log and streams them to downstream consumers in near-real time. Tools such as Debezium implement CDC without modifying the application or adding significant load to the source database.
terms.example: In a hotel reservation system, Debezium captures every change to the MySQL room-inventory table and publishes it to Redis, keeping the in-memory inventory cache eventually consistent without a polling loop or dual-write in application code.
terms.howItWorks:
The database already writes every change to a log before it applies it, such as the MySQL binlog or the Postgres write-ahead log. A CDC connector acts like a read-only replica. It connects, asks for the log from a given position, and decodes each record into an event with the table, operation, and the before and after row images.

With Debezium, the connector runs inside Kafka Connect. It first takes a consistent snapshot of existing rows, then switches to streaming the log. It stores its position, an LSN in Postgres or a binlog file and offset in MySQL, in a Kafka offset topic. After a crash it resumes from that position.

Each event goes to a topic named per table, keyed by primary key so changes to one row stay in order. Consumers read the topic to update caches, search indexes, or a warehouse.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Applications make no dual writes, so the database stays the single source of truth. Polling by `updated_at` misses hard deletes and adds query load, and CDC catches both.
- Latency is usually tens to hundreds of milliseconds, but consumers are eventually consistent and may read stale data.
- Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once needs extra work in the sink.
- The log reader holds log files on the source. A stuck connector keeps the WAL from being recycled and can fill the disk.
terms.failureModes:
- The connector is down longer than log retention. Symptom is a resume failure with a missing position error. Mitigate by alerting on connector lag and triggering a fresh snapshot.
- A Postgres replication slot goes unread. WAL piles up on the primary until the disk is full. Mitigate by monitoring `pg_replication_slots` retained size and setting `max_slot_wal_keep_size`.
- A schema change such as dropping a column breaks downstream consumers. Symptom is deserialisation errors in the consumer. Mitigate with a schema registry and compatibility checks.
- Events for the same row land on different partitions after a key change, so order flips. Mitigate by keying on the primary key.

terms.definition: A bookkeeping method where every financial transaction is recorded in at least two accounts—one debited and one credited—so that the sum of all ledger entries always equals zero. This constraint provides end-to-end traceability of money movement and makes inconsistencies or fraud far easier to detect.
terms.example: When a buyer pays a seller $1, the ledger records a $1 debit on the buyer account and a $1 credit on the seller account; the net sum remains zero, giving the finance team a complete audit trail for every dollar that moves through the system.
terms.howItWorks:
A ledger is an append-only table of entries. Each entry names an account, an amount, a direction of debit or credit, and a transaction ID. All entries sharing a transaction ID must sum to zero, with debits counted positive and credits negative.

A payment of $1 from a buyer to a seller writes two rows in one database transaction. One debits the buyer's account and one credits the seller's. If either insert fails, the transaction rolls back and neither exists. Entries are never updated or deleted. A mistake is fixed by a new reversing transaction.

An account balance is the sum of its entries, often cached in a balance table that is updated in the same transaction. A reconciliation job checks that the global sum is 0 and that cached balances match the sums of entries.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Every movement of money has a traceable counterpart, so a missing or duplicated amount shows up as a nonzero sum. A single-row balance update gives no such check.
- Write volume doubles, at least two rows per transaction. A split payment with fees and tax may need four or more.
- Append-only history makes audits and replay easy, but storage grows forever, so old rows need archiving by partition.
- Hot accounts, like a platform fee account, take a write on every transaction and become a lock bottleneck. Sharding the account into sub-accounts spreads that load but adds a sum on read.
terms.failureModes:
- A retry of a failed API call posts the transaction twice. Symptom is a customer charged twice, though the ledger still sums to zero. Mitigate with an idempotency key under a unique constraint.
- Entries are written in separate transactions and the process dies between them. Symptom is a nonzero sum. Mitigate by writing both legs in one DB transaction and running a reconciliation query.
- Mixed currencies or rounding put cents in the wrong place. Symptom is a sum off by 0.01. Mitigate with integer minor units and one currency per transaction.

terms.definition: A third-party company (such as Stripe, Braintree, or Square) that connects merchants to card schemes like Visa and Mastercard to move money between buyer and seller accounts. PSPs also offer hosted payment pages that collect and store card details directly, shielding merchants from PCI-DSS compliance obligations.
terms.example: After a user submits card details on a PSP-hosted page, the PSP charges the card and sends the result back to the merchant's payment service via a webhook—containing only a token, never raw card data—so the merchant never touches sensitive financial information.
terms.howItWorks:
The merchant's backend creates a payment object with the PSP API, passing an amount, a currency, and an idempotency key. The PSP returns a client secret. The browser loads the PSP's hosted fields or checkout page, so the card number goes from the user's device to the PSP and never touches the merchant's servers. The PSP replaces the card with a token and sends an authorization request through the acquirer and the card network to the issuing bank.

The issuer approves or declines in a second or two. Funds are only reserved at that point. Capture later moves them, and settlement to the merchant's bank takes one to several days. The PSP reports each state change by a signed webhook (for example `payment_intent.succeeded`), and the merchant verifies the HMAC signature and updates the order.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Hosted card fields keep the merchant at the lightest PCI scope (SAQ A). The checkout design is limited to what the PSP allows.
- Typical fees are around 2.9% plus a fixed amount per card charge. Direct acquiring can be cheaper at large volume but you take on compliance and risk tooling.
- Building on one PSP is fast. Moving later means migrating stored tokens, which needs the PSP's cooperation, so some teams add a thin abstraction layer from the start.
- The PSP provides fraud scoring and 3-D Secure. False declines still lose sales, and you have limited insight into why.
terms.failureModes:
- The client retries a charge after a network timeout and the customer is charged twice. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on every create call and store it with the order.
- Webhooks arrive out of order or twice. An order is marked paid, then reverted to pending. Make handlers idempotent by event ID and check the object's current state from the API.
- The webhook endpoint is down for a few hours. The PSP retries with backoff, then stops. Orders sit unpaid despite the charge. Run a periodic reconciliation job against the PSP's list of payments.
- Webhook signatures are not verified. Anyone can post a fake success event and receive goods. Verify the signature over the raw body with the endpoint secret.

terms.definition: A process in which a payment system compares its internal ledger and wallet records against an external PSP settlement file to detect discrepancies. Mismatches are classified as auto-correctable via a standard procedure, manually correctable by the finance team, or unclassifiable for deeper investigation.
terms.example: In the Payment System design, a nightly reconciliation job compares the internal ledger against the PSP's settlement file; any payment the PSP recorded as successful but the internal ledger never confirmed is flagged for the finance team to resolve before the next business day.
terms.howItWorks:
After the PSP closes a settlement period, it publishes a file, often CSV or SFTP-delivered, listing every transaction with its ID, amount, currency, fee and status. A batch job loads that file and the internal ledger entries for the same period and joins them on the PSP reference.

Each row lands in one of a few buckets. Matched in both with equal amounts is fine. In the PSP file but missing internally means a payment succeeded but the callback was lost. In the ledger but missing at the PSP means the internal system recorded success that never happened. Present in both with different amounts or statuses is a mismatch.

Known patterns trigger automatic fixes, such as replaying a lost webhook. Everything else becomes a ticket for finance.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Catches money errors that real-time checks miss, such as lost callbacks and double captures, but only after a delay of hours or a day.
- Automatic correction clears most routine breaks. A wrong rule can write bad ledger entries at scale, so each auto-fix needs an audit trail.
- Matching on amount and time instead of a unique reference handles messy PSP data but produces false matches. A stable reference ID is far better.
- Daily batch is simple. Streaming reconciliation shortens detection time but needs idempotent event handling and more infrastructure.
terms.failureModes:
- Time zone mismatch between the PSP cut-off, often UTC, and the ledger date puts transactions near midnight in different days, giving a flood of false breaks. Normalize to UTC timestamps.
- Currency rounding or fee deduction differs by a cent per row, so thousands of rows mismatch. Compare in minor units and allow a documented tolerance for fees.
- Duplicate rows in the PSP file, from a re-sent file, are counted twice and the totals drift. Deduplicate on the PSP reference and track file checksums.
- Late-arriving refunds and chargebacks appear in a later file and look like unexplained differences. Carry unmatched items forward for several days before escalating.
terms.codeSnippet:
-- internal ledger vs PSP settlement for one day
SELECT COALESCE(l.psp_ref, s.psp_ref) AS ref,
       l.amount_minor AS ledger_amt, s.amount_minor AS psp_amt,
       CASE
         WHEN l.psp_ref IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_ledger'
         WHEN s.psp_ref IS NULL THEN 'missing_at_psp'
         ELSE 'amount_mismatch'
       END AS break_type
FROM ledger_entries l
FULL OUTER JOIN psp_settlement s ON s.psp_ref = l.psp_ref
WHERE l.psp_ref IS NULL OR s.psp_ref IS NULL
   OR l.amount_minor <> s.amount_minor;

terms.definition: A data structure that stores unique elements each paired with a floating-point score, maintaining the elements in sorted order by score at all times. Redis implements it internally as a hash map for O(1) member-to-score lookup combined with a skip list for O(log N) ranked access and range queries.
terms.example: A real-time gaming leaderboard for 25 million monthly users stores all player scores in a Redis sorted set: `ZINCRBY leaderboard_feb_2021 1 'alice'` updates a score in O(log N), while `ZREVRANGE leaderboard_feb_2021 0 9 WITHSCORES` retrieves the top 10 players in a single command.
terms.howItWorks:
A Redis sorted set keeps two structures over the same members. A hash table maps member to score, so `ZSCORE` is O(1). A skip list ordered by score, then by member name, gives ordered access. `ZADD` and `ZINCRBY` update both, each in O(log N).

Rank queries use span counters stored on skip list links. `ZRANK` sums spans along the search path instead of walking every node. `ZRANGE` finds the start in O(log N) and then reads M elements by following level-0 links, for O(log N + M). Small sets under 128 entries use a compact listpack encoding instead, which saves memory until the set grows past the limit.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Updates and rank lookups cost O(log N), so a leaderboard of 25 million entries answers top-10 in microseconds, but all data must fit in RAM.
- The hash plus skip list roughly doubles per-member memory over a plain hash, about 100 bytes of overhead per entry.
- Scores are 64-bit doubles. Integers above 2^53 lose precision.
- A single sorted set lives on one shard in Redis Cluster. Splitting by key helps throughput but makes global rank hard.
terms.failureModes:
- One huge set becomes a hot key on a single node. CPU saturates on that shard. Split by time or bucket and merge top results in the app.
- `ZRANGE 0 -1` on millions of members blocks the single-threaded server for hundreds of milliseconds. Other commands stall. Page with small ranges or use `ZSCAN`.
- Ties compare by member lexicographic order, so equal scores rank in a surprising way. Encode a timestamp in the score if tie order matters.
terms.codeSnippet:
# leaderboard commands
ZINCRBY leaderboard_feb_2021 10 alice     # O(log N)
ZADD leaderboard_feb_2021 NX 0 bob
ZREVRANGE leaderboard_feb_2021 0 9 WITHSCORES   # top 10
ZREVRANK leaderboard_feb_2021 alice       # 0-based position
ZSCORE leaderboard_feb_2021 alice
ZCARD leaderboard_feb_2021
EXPIRE leaderboard_feb_2021 2764800       # drop after 32 days

terms.definition: A probabilistic data structure built from a sorted linked list augmented with multiple levels of forward pointers, enabling O(log N) average-case search, insertion, and deletion without the rotation complexity of balanced trees. Higher-level pointers allow large portions of the list to be bypassed during traversal.
terms.example: In a sorted set with 64 nodes, a plain linked list requires visiting up to 62 nodes to locate a value, whereas a skip list with multi-level indexes reaches the same value in roughly 11 hops—the foundation of Redis sorted-set performance.
terms.howItWorks:
A skip list is a sorted linked list where each node also joins higher-level lists. On insert, a coin flip decides the node's height. Each extra level occurs with probability p, which is 0.25 in Redis, so roughly one in four nodes reaches level 2.

Search starts at the top level of the head node and moves right while the next key is smaller than the target. When the next key is too large, it drops one level and continues. At level 0 it lands on the target or its insertion point. Expected steps are about `log(1/p) N`. Insert records the last node visited per level, then splices the new node in at each of its levels. No rebalancing is needed.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Expected O(log N) with simple code. A red-black tree needs rotations and is hard to make lock-free.
- Concurrent skip lists, as in Java `ConcurrentSkipListMap` or LSM memtables, need only local pointer updates, so writers rarely block each other.
- Memory is about 1.33 pointers per node extra at p = 0.25, and nodes scatter in memory, which hurts CPU cache locality compared with a B-tree.
- Performance is probabilistic. A bad random run can raise latency, though the chance falls fast with N.
terms.failureModes:
- A weak or seeded-identically random generator gives skewed heights, so search degrades toward O(N). Latency creeps up under load. Use a good PRNG and cap max level, 32 in Redis.
- Concurrent insertion with a buggy lock order loses nodes or loops at level links. Operations hang. Use lock-free CAS patterns from a tested library.
- Memory grows with pointer overhead on tiny entries. A memtable with millions of small keys takes more RAM than expected. Use arena allocation and measure per-node bytes.

terms.definition: A real-time record of all outstanding buy and sell limit orders for a security, organized by price level. Each price level holds a queue of orders; the best bid (highest buy price) and best ask (lowest sell price) define the current spread. An efficient implementation pairs a hash map for O(1) price-level lookup with a doubly-linked list for O(1) order addition and cancellation.
terms.example: When a large market buy order consumes all sell orders at $100 from the order book, those entries are removed and the best ask rises to the next populated price level, widening the spread and reflecting real-time supply-demand dynamics to all market participants.
terms.howItWorks:
An order book keeps two sides. Bids sort by price descending and asks ascending. Each price level holds a FIFO queue of resting orders, which gives price-time priority. A hash map from order ID to its list node lets a cancel jump straight to the order.

When a limit order arrives, the matching engine compares it with the best price on the opposite side. If it crosses, it fills against the head of that level's queue, order by order, until it is filled or no longer crosses. The remainder rests at its price. Cancel removes the node in O(1). The best bid and ask are cached pointers, updated when a level empties.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Hash map by price plus doubly linked queue gives O(1) add and cancel, but finding the next populated level after one empties needs a sorted structure, which costs O(log P) in a tree.
- Single-threaded matching per symbol gives strict ordering and no locks, at the price of one core as the throughput ceiling per instrument, often hundreds of thousands of orders per second.
- Keeping the book in memory gives microsecond latency. Durability needs an append-only event log for replay.
- Pro-rata matching can replace FIFO but makes queue logic more complex.
terms.failureModes:
- Crash with no event log loses resting orders. Clients see their orders vanish. Journal every command before applying and replay on restart.
- A burst of cancels after news makes queues churn. Memory and latency jump. Pool order objects and preallocate.
- Floating-point prices produce level mismatches such as 100.1 vs 100.10000001. Orders fail to match. Store prices as integer ticks.

# book per symbol: price -> FIFO queue of orders
bids = SortedDict()           # best = max key
asks = SortedDict()           # best = min key
orders = {}                   # order_id -> (side, price, node)

def add_limit(side, price, qty, oid):
    qty = match(side, price, qty)            # fill against opposite side
    if qty > 0:
        node = book(side).setdefault(price, DList()).append((oid, qty))
        orders[oid] = (side, price, node)

def cancel(oid):
    side, price, node = orders.pop(oid)
    book(side)[price].remove(node)           # O(1)

terms.definition: The core component of a stock exchange that maintains the order book for each traded symbol and pairs compatible buy and sell limit orders to produce execution fills. Correct operation requires strict determinism—identical inputs must always produce identical outputs—so that replayed event logs can reconstruct the exact sequence of trades.
terms.example: In the Stock Exchange design, the matching engine, order manager, and sequencer all share a single server and exchange events through a memory-mapped file in /dev/shm, achieving tens-of-microseconds round-trip latency instead of the tens-of-milliseconds typical of networked services; this handles the 215,000 peak QPS target.
terms.howItWorks:
For each symbol the engine keeps an order book with two sides. Bids are sorted by price descending and asks by price ascending. Each price level holds a FIFO queue of orders, which gives price-time priority. A hash map from order ID to its node allows cancels in constant time.

When a limit buy arrives, the engine compares its price with the best ask. If the buy price is at or above that ask, it matches against the oldest order at that level, emits a fill for the smaller quantity, and repeats until the order is filled or no ask crosses. Any rest is added to the bids at its price.

The engine is single-threaded per symbol and reads a sequenced input stream. Every event gets a sequence number before it is processed. Replaying the same stream from a snapshot rebuilds the same book and the same fills.
terms.tradeoffs:
- A single thread per book needs no locks and gives deterministic results. Throughput is bound by one core, so scale comes from sharding symbols across engines.
- Keeping everything in memory gives microsecond matching but needs an event log for recovery. Snapshots plus replay make restart time a function of log length.
- Co-locating the sequencer, order manager, and engine on one host removes network hops. It also puts them in one failure domain, so a standby must replay the same stream.
- Price levels in a sorted structure give `O(log n)` insertion. Array-indexed levels over a tick grid give `O(1)` and use more memory.
terms.failureModes:
- Nondeterminism creeps in, such as reading wall-clock time or iterating a hash map in random order. Symptom is a replica whose book differs from the primary after replay. Mitigate by using only sequence numbers and ordered structures, and by comparing book hashes between replicas.
- A garbage collection pause or a stray allocation on the hot path adds milliseconds. Symptom is p99 latency spikes. Mitigate with preallocated pools and a non-GC language or tuned runtime.
- The primary fails between writing a fill and publishing it. Symptom is a client with a fill the market data feed does not show. Mitigate by publishing only from the replicated log.

terms.definition: A distributed transaction protocol that divides a transaction into two independent phases: a Try phase that reserves or modifies resources in each participating database as separate local transactions, followed by a Confirm or Cancel phase that either finalizes or reverses those changes via compensating transactions. Unlike 2PC, no long-held locks span a network round-trip.
terms.example: To transfer $1 from account A to account C across two database shards, the Try phase debits A's shard (local transaction); if successful, the Confirm phase credits C's shard (separate local transaction). A failure in Try triggers a Cancel that reverses A's debit—ensuring money is neither lost nor duplicated.
terms.howItWorks:
TCC splits each participant's work into three operations that the service itself exposes. Try reserves resources and checks invariants, for example moving $1 from `balance` to a `frozen` column on account A. Confirm turns the reservation into the final state. Cancel releases it.

A coordinator calls Try on every participant. If all return success, it calls Confirm on all. If any fails, it calls Cancel on those that succeeded. Each call is its own short local transaction, so no database lock spans the network.

The coordinator logs the transaction state durably, then retries Confirm or Cancel until each participant acknowledges. Because of retries, all three operations must be idempotent. A Cancel may also arrive before its Try (empty rollback), and the participant must handle it.
terms.tradeoffs:
- No locks are held across services, so throughput stays high compared to 2PC, where participants hold locks through the prepare phase.
- Every service must implement three endpoints and a reservation model, which is much more code than a plain local transaction.
- Reserved resources are visible to others (frozen balance), so you must decide how reads treat them.
- Isolation is weaker than 2PC. Another request can observe the intermediate reserved state between Try and Confirm.
terms.failureModes:
- Cancel arrives before Try because of a network delay, then Try executes and holds the reservation forever. Record cancelled transaction IDs and reject a late Try (null rollback guard).
- Confirm is retried after success and credits twice. Store a transaction ID per operation and make Confirm a no-op on repeat.
- The coordinator crashes after Try succeeded. Reservations sit frozen. Persist state and run a recovery job, with a reservation timeout that triggers Cancel.
terms.codeSnippet:
# Account service: three idempotent endpoints, keyed by tx_id
def try_debit(tx_id, acct, amt):
    with db.transaction():
        if cancelled(tx_id): return "REJECTED"   # late Try guard
        db.exec("UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-%s, frozen=frozen+%s "
                "WHERE id=%s AND bal>=%s", amt, amt, acct, amt)
        db.exec("INSERT INTO tcc_log(tx_id,state) VALUES(%s,'TRIED') "
                "ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING", tx_id)
def confirm_debit(tx_id): ...  # frozen -= amt, state='CONFIRMED'
def cancel_debit(tx_id): ...   # bal += amt, frozen -= amt, state='CANCELLED'

terms.definition: A technique to prevent write hotspots in a partitioned data store by appending a computed shard suffix (e.g., `key % N`) to the natural partition key, distributing writes across N physical partitions. The trade-off is that reads require a scatter-gather query across all N shards, with results merged in the application.
terms.example: In a DynamoDB gaming leaderboard partitioned by month, appending `user_id % 8` to each partition key spreads writes across 8 shards; fetching the top-10 players then requires querying all 8 shards and merging the results—with the optimal shard count determined by benchmarking write vs. read latency.
terms.howItWorks:
A hot partition key concentrates writes on one physical partition, which has a throughput ceiling, such as 1,000 write units per second in DynamoDB. To spread the load, the writer appends a suffix to the natural key, for example `2026-10#3`. The suffix comes from a hash of the item, like `user_id % 8`, or from a random number when ordering does not matter.

With 8 suffixes, the same logical key lives in 8 partitions, each taking about one eighth of the writes. A write needs no extra lookup, since the suffix is computed from data the writer already has.

A read must visit every suffix. The reader issues 8 queries in parallel, takes the top results from each, and merges them in the application. For a top-10 board that means pulling 10 from each shard and sorting 80 items.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Write capacity grows nearly linearly with shard count. 8 shards lift a 1,000 per second cap to roughly 8,000.
- Every read becomes a scatter-gather of N queries. Read cost and tail latency rise, since the slowest shard decides the response time.
- A deterministic suffix like `user_id % 8` lets you read one user's rows from one shard. A random suffix spreads writes more evenly but forces you to query all shards even for one user.
- Changing N later means rewriting or double-reading existing items, so choose it with headroom. Benchmark both write and read latency before fixing a number.
terms.failureModes:
- The shard choice is skewed, such as a few power users all landing on the same suffix. Symptom is throttling on one partition while others idle. Mitigate by hashing a high-cardinality field and checking per-shard metrics.
- One shard query fails or times out during a gather. The merged result silently omits its data. Symptom is a leaderboard missing top players. Mitigate by failing the read or flagging a partial result.
- N is raised from 8 to 16 and old items still sit under the old suffixes. Symptom is missing rows in reads. Mitigate by reading both layouts during migration, or by backfilling.

terms.definition: A protocol for uploading large objects by splitting them into independently uploadable chunks, each identified by a part number and verified with an ETag (typically an MD5 checksum). After all parts are uploaded, a completion call reassembles them into the final object server-side, allowing parallel uploads and retrying only failed chunks without restarting the full transfer.
terms.example: Uploading a 5 GB video to an S3-like store initiates a multipart upload that returns a unique upload ID; the client splits the file into 50 MB parts uploaded in parallel, then calls complete-multipart-upload with all part numbers and ETags—after which the data store reassembles the object and a garbage-collector reclaims the orphaned part chunks.
terms.howItWorks:
The client first calls initiate, and the store returns an `UploadId`. The client cuts the file into parts. S3 requires each part except the last to be at least 5 MiB, allows up to 10,000 parts, and caps an object at 5 TiB. Each part is sent in its own `UploadPart` request with the upload ID and a part number from 1 to 10,000. The response carries an `ETag` for that part.

Parts can go in parallel, in any order, and a failed one is simply sent again under the same number. When all are in, the client calls complete with the list of part numbers and ETags. The store checks the list, concatenates the parts in number order, and publishes the object atomically. Until completion, nothing is visible as an object, but the stored parts still count toward storage cost.
terms.tradeoffs:
- Parallel parts can saturate a fast link, often 5 to 10 times a single stream. Each part is an extra HTTP request, so tiny parts waste time on overhead.
- A failed part costs only that part's retransmission. A single `PUT` of 5 GB restarts from byte zero on a drop.
- Unfinished uploads keep billing for stored parts. A lifecycle rule to abort incomplete uploads after 7 days handles it.
- The multipart ETag is not the MD5 of the whole file. It is the MD5 of the part MD5s plus a part count, so you need separate checksums for end-to-end verification.
terms.failureModes:
- A client crashes mid-upload and never completes or aborts. Orphaned parts accumulate and bills grow quietly. Add an `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle rule and a periodic list-uploads audit.
- Parts are smaller than the 5 MiB minimum. Complete fails with `EntityTooSmall`. Choose part size as max(5 MiB, file size / 10,000).
- Complete lists a wrong or stale ETag after a part was re-uploaded. The call fails with `InvalidPart`. Record the ETag of the last successful attempt for each part number.
- Parallelism set too high opens hundreds of sockets and drives memory use. Cap concurrency at around 8 to 16 parts and stream from disk.
terms.codeSnippet:
# 1. Start the upload and note the UploadId
aws s3api create-multipart-upload --bucket media --key video.mp4
# 2. Send a part (repeat for 1..N, in parallel if you like)
aws s3api upload-part --bucket media --key video.mp4 \
  --part-number 1 --body part-aa --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID
# 3. Assemble using the ETags returned above
aws s3api complete-multipart-upload --bucket media --key video.mp4 \
  --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID --multipart-upload file://parts.json
# Cleanup if the client gives up
aws s3api abort-multipart-upload --bucket media --key video.mp4 --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID
